# BLO-35486 / BLO-38096 — order Job teardown so a run's Secrets outlive the pod that mounts them

Changed files: `src/server/execute.ts`, `src/server/execute.test.ts`,
`src/server/job-manifest.test.ts`. Landed across
[#2099](https://github.com/Blockcast/paperclip/pull/2099) and
[#2116](https://github.com/Blockcast/paperclip/pull/2116) (the latter's commits
are carried on this branch).

## The original defect ([BLO-35486](https://paperclip.blockcast.net/BLO/issues/BLO-35486))

Every teardown path deleted the Job with `propagationPolicy: Background` — which
returns before the GC removes the pod — then deleted the per-run Secrets
immediately, so a pod still mid-image-pull started its container into
`secret "ac-<run>-env" not found`. Now: delete pods, poll until the API reports
none, delete the Job, then the Secrets; if a pod outlives the 60s budget neither
the Job nor the Secrets are deleted (deleting the Job reaps them via
`ownerReference`). This covers the `skipCleanup` and `retainJobs` paths, which
kept a pod alive on purpose and deleted its Secrets anyway. The keepalive
external-cancel path bypassed `cleanupJob()` entirely and is covered separately
by `teardownCancelledJob()`, which deliberately does *not* fail closed, because a
cancelled run only settles on a Job 404 and `completionTimeoutMs` may be 0.

Also raised the `podStartTimeoutSec` default 600 → 1800: a cold 3.3 GB
agent-image pull under 8-way contention measured 11m12s–12m36s, so the old budget
sat below the observed floor and failed the first wave of runs on every node
after each image bump.

## Secret ownership ahead of the launch-ack aborts (Ally review on #2099)

Moved the per-run Secrets' `ownerReference` patch above the two launch-ack abort
paths (no UID / no ack wired, and ack throws). Those paths run before the Job is
acknowledged, and since the change above they keep the Secrets when a pod
outlives teardown on the promise that Job GC collects them; with the patch still
below them the Secrets had no owner, and the adapter has no Secret reaper, so the
credential-bearing `<job>-env` Secret was orphaned for good. Also pinned the
concurrency guard's `{ waitForPods: false }` reap with a test: that loop sits
outside the 15s guard timeout, so dropping the opt-out would add up to 60s per
stale Job at every run start.

## Observability of the teardown poll (second Ally pass on #2099)

Log the first non-404 pod-list failure in `deleteJobPodsAndWait`, once. A
persistent RBAC/5xx on the teardown-confirmation poll retried silently to the
deadline and then failed closed on the same path as a genuinely wedged pod, so
the two were indistinguishable in a postmortem while both left the Job and
Secrets behind. Also recorded the `POD_TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` invariant at its
declaration: it must exceed the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, which
`buildJobManifest` does not set (so pods ride the K8s 30s default), and the two
values live in different files — raising the grace period past 60s would make
every teardown hit the timeout and retain Job and Secrets with no reaper.

## 3-state teardown outcome ([BLO-38096](https://paperclip.blockcast.net/BLO/issues/BLO-38096))

Split `deleteJobPodsAndWait`'s `boolean` into a `PodTeardownOutcome`
(`gone` / `alive` / `unobserved`). The single `false` conflated *pods are still
there* with *no pod list ever succeeded*, which cost two things. Both retention
warnings said "pod(s) … still present" in a branch where nothing had been seen —
the poll had failed to look. And `teardownCancelledJob`'s fail-open applied to
both, on a comment asserting "the pod delete has already been issued by that
point": false when one apiserver fault denies both verbs, because a non-404
`deleteCollection` failure is swallowed and falls through to the poll. It then
deleted the Job with the delete never issued and nothing observed, reaping the
run Secrets via `ownerReference` GC under a pod that can still start — the
original defect on the cancel path. The cancel path now fails open only on
`alive` (the apiserver answered, so the pod is Terminating) and closed on
`unobserved`; `cleanupJob` fails closed on both, unchanged. `unobserved` means
*no* poll ever succeeded, not *the last one failed*, so a late blip after clean
reads cannot flip a sound fail-open into the hang the fail-open exists to
prevent. Also made the `POD_TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` cross-file invariant a test
rather than prose: `job-manifest.test.ts` now asserts the rendered pod spec
leaves `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` unset.

## `undeleted`: gate the fail-open on an accepted delete (Ally review on #2116)

Added a fourth outcome, `undeleted`, so the cancel path's fail-open is gated on
the pod delete actually being accepted rather than inferred from the poll.
`alive` was returned whenever a list succeeded, but `list` and `deletecollection`
are separate verbs: a Role granting pods `list` without `deletecollection`, or a
5xx on the delete alone, swallowed the delete failure, then saw the never-deleted
(not Terminating) pod and returned `alive`, and `teardownCancelledJob` deleted
the Job, so `ownerReference` GC reaped the run Secrets under a pod that could
still start. `deleteJobPodsAndWait` now records whether `deleteCollection` was
accepted and returns `alive` only then; a pod still listed after a refused delete
is `undeleted`, which `teardownCancelledJob` retains like `unobserved` and
`cleanupJob` retains like every non-`gone` outcome.

## Retry the refused delete each poll (two Ally findings on #2116 at `5b596d19`)

`deleteJobPodsAndWait` now re-issues the pod `deleteCollection` on every poll
until it is accepted, instead of once before the poll. Issued once, a single
transient fault (one 503) latched `undeleted` for the whole teardown,
indistinguishable from a persistent denial, and `teardownCancelledJob` retained
the Job over a pod that was never deleted and kept running. Now `undeleted` means
refused for the whole budget, as its doc claims, and a transient fault heals into
`alive`; the failure is still logged once, not per poll. Also documented the
pod-side cost of retaining on `undeleted`: deleting the Job with
`propagationPolicy: Background` hands pod removal to the
kube-controller-manager garbage collector, which acts under its own credentials,
so retaining gives up the last lever that stops the pod when this ServiceAccount
cannot — and the "needs a total read outage" justification applies to
`unobserved` only.

## Guard the teardown logs the cancel path has no catch above (Ally review at `a6ddd2b2`)

Guarded the two `await onLog(...)` calls inside `deleteJobPodsAndWait` with
`.catch(() => undefined)` — the last unguarded ones on the cancel path, which has
no supervision above it: the keepalive fires the teardown from a
`void (async () => {…})()` with no `.catch`, and `teardownCancelledJob` awaits
bare. A rejecting `onLog` therefore unwound past the outcome computation before
`deleteJobOnly` ran, so the Job was never deleted, `waitForJobCompletion` never
saw its 404, and the run hung — the exact hang the `alive` fail-open exists to
prevent, reached by the logging of the fault, with no warning line emitted
because the rejection *is* the log attempt. Both guards match the idiom
`teardownCancelledJob` already applies to its own two logs.

The delete failure is now reported **twice at most**: the first, which explains
why the retry started, and the final one at the deadline when the cause changed
(a 503 on poll 1 degrading into a persistent 403 reported the 503 while the
`undeleted` verdict was caused by the 403, so the logged cause and the cause of
the outcome disagreed). Emitted at the deadline rather than per poll, so a stable
error still logs once. And `cleanupJob`'s retention warning now names the
pod-side retain cost on the `undeleted` branch: `leaving Job and run Secrets for
K8s GC` reads as deferred cleanup, but on `undeleted` nothing was ever marked for
deletion, so the pod is not Terminating and keeps running until a later run's
concurrency guard reaps the Job. Five guards, each mutation-tested individually:
dropping any one `.catch`, suppressing the deadline line, or collapsing the
retain-cost clause turns the suite red on its own.
